title: Dynamic Preference Logic of Preference Lifting
authors: Xiaochen Chang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In preference logic, preference is modeled as a binary relation between possible worlds. When we discuss preference relations between propositions, we also need to consider how to lift this relation between possible worlds to propositions. Here, propositions are usually represented by their extensions, that is, sets of possible worlds. There are several choices of lifting scheme: for example, one may require even the worst world in one set to be better than the best world in another, or merely require that every world in one set have some better world in the other. The framing effect in behavioral economics shows that the lifting scheme can change with the way a question is posed or with psychological factors. This paper proves that such changes cannot be reduced to changes in preferences between possible worlds. Accordingly, we treat the lifting scheme as an independent dimension of evaluation and use a hybrid language to describe switches between lifting schemes. We thereby present a language for preference logic with dynamic lifting and prove its soundness and completeness.

title: Littlestone Dimension and Its Dual
authors: Pooya Hatami, Chavdar Lalov
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26721v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The dual Littlestone dimension of a concept class $\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$, $\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H}):=\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H}^*)$, is the Littlestone dimension of the dual class $\mathcal{H}^*$, obtained by exchanging the roles of domain points and hypotheses. A classical result of Shelah implies that $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})$ and $\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H})$ are finite simultaneously, and quantitative results of Hodges [Mathematika, 1981] imply the doubly exponential bound $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\le 2^{2^{O(\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H}))}}$. Malliaris and Moran [Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 2024] asked whether this bound is optimal. We answer this by proving the improved bound \[ \operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\le 2^{O(\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H})^2)}. \] An exponential dependence is necessary, as witnessed by the class of all binary hypotheses on a finite domain.

title: Learning under Bounded Manipulation for Quadratic Incentive Design
authors: Arda G\"u\c{c}l\"u, Subhonmesh Bose, Tamer Ba\c{s}ar
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study a repeated quadratic incentive design game in which a leader learns a follower's private type from noisy observations of the follower's actions and uses her estimates in an affine incentive rule. The follower knows the leader's learning policy, which incorporates past observations to produce estimates of the follower's type, and can deviate from his myopic best response to influence the leader's future estimates. We ask how the follower's ability to manipulate these observations affects the leader's performance. Under a manipulation budget $C_T$ constraining the expected cumulative squared deviation of the follower's actions from his myopic best response, we establish a minimax regret rate of order $\max\{\log T, \min\{C_T,T\}\}$ for approximately rational followers. Our information-theoretic lower bound applies to a general class of causal estimation and manipulation policies for the leader and the follower. We provide a simple learning policy that achieves the lower bound. Finally, we show that under a fixed learning rule, increasing the manipulation budget of the follower can counterintuitively reduce the leader's regret.

title: Exploring Early Vulnerability Analysis via Automatic Identification of Vulnerability-Introducing Commits
authors: Weiliang Qi, Shu Wang, Youpeng Li, Ela Guo, Xinda Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26739v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Developing effective vulnerability analysis techniques requires high-quality datasets that capture how vulnerabilities appear and evolve in real software codebase. Existing datasets, however, typically label as vulnerable only the code immediately preceding vulnerability-fixing commits (VFCs), overlooking the earlier versions in which vulnerabilities were first introduced and subsequently evolved. This practice limits both dataset coverage and our understanding of whether current detectors can identify vulnerabilities during their early, latent stages. In this paper, we present three manually annotated datasets of vulnerability-introducing commits (VICs) based on recent CVEs and widely used open-source projects. We further propose D-SZZ, a data state-aware VIC identification framework that analyzes security-fixing patterns and performs vulnerability scope slicing to recover the semantics implied by a fix. Experimental results demonstrate that D-SZZ outperforms existing SZZ and LLM-based baselines in identifying VICs. In addition, we evaluate six representative vulnerability detectors and find that models trained only on pre-VFC code struggle with original vulnerabilities, while incorporating early-stage samples improves detection performance. We also show that D-SZZ improves downstream vulnerable-version identification, and use it to uncover 16 inaccurate affected-version records in the NVD, all of which were officially confirmed and updated.

title: DNN-Assisted Deterministic Policy Learning for Adaptive IRS-NOMA-OWC Networks
authors: Ahrar N. Hamad, Ahmad A. Qidan, Taisir E. H. El-Gorashi, Jaafar M. H. Elmirghani
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26742v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) has been considered a promising technology in optical wireless communication (OWC) networks due to its potential to overcome the line-of-sight (LoS) blockage issue and enhance coverage. In this paper, a dynamic IRS-assisted indoor non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-OWC network is modeled, and an optimization problem is formulated to maximize the sum rate subject to the quality-of-service (QoS) requirements of multiple mobile users, by jointly optimizing the power allocation and the IRS mirror orientations, from which the user's decoding order is induced rather than being fixed. Since the problem is non-convex and the channel conditions vary with user mobility, conventional optimization methods may incur considerable computational overhead. Therefore, a two-stage deep neural network-deep reinforcement learning (DNN-DRL) framework is proposed. In the first stage, the DNN estimates the user's positions and orientations in real time, removing the need for perfect knowledge of the user state. In the second stage, a deterministic policy gradient (DPG)-based DRL algorithm uses these estimates to jointly optimize the power allocation and IRS mirror orientations, with the decoding order updated according to the resulting effective channel gains. The results show that the proposed framework approaches the performance upper bounds and outperforms standard DRL algorithms, conventional optimization methods, and deployments without IRS in terms of sum rate and fairness, while achieving faster convergence. Furthermore, online adaptation of the decoding order maintains higher QoS satisfaction than a fixed decoding order, particularly under high user mobility.

title: Suffused NV-FETs for Reconfigurable Hardware
authors: Alexander J. Edwards, Son T. Le, Thomas Broadfoot, Samuel W. LaGasse, Collin R. Sanborn, Nicholas A. Blumenschein, Aubrey T. Hanbicki, Adam L. Friedman
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26771v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We define a new category of programmable device, the non-volatile (NV) suffused FET, in response to recent advances in photo- [1]-[3] and e-beam doping [4] We demonstrate that the writing mechanism of suffused NV FETs largely reduces the required access circuitry compared with other NV switches, and that with available configurations as a closed switch, open switch, NFET, or PFET, the suffused NV FET is ideal for configuration storage in reconfigurable arrays, reducing FET count in one case by 84.5%.

title: Incentive Compatible Mechanisms for Sequential Fair Resource Allocation with Private Demands
authors: Ramtin Salamat, Sean R. Sinclair, Seyed M. R. Iravani
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26800v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study a strategic variant of the canonical online fair allocation problem, where a planner must sequentially allocate a divisible resource to agents with privately known demands. At each stage, the planner announces an allocation rule, the agent reports their demand, and the planner allocates resources according to the rule and the reported demand. Unlike the standard model, we allow agents to strategically misreport their needs, as can arise in nonprofit settings where demand is self-reported and monetary transfers are unavailable. We characterize the structure of incentive-compatible (IC) allocation rules in this model, and use this to identify conditions under which the optimal mechanism has a simple cap structure. We then develop an approximation method for the optimal IC mechanism through a careful reduction of the discretized dynamic program to a longest-path problem on a directed acyclic graph. Numerical experiments show that ignoring strategic reporting can be substantially more costly than imposing incentive compatibility.

title: A Unified Framework for Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection and Alert Correlation
authors: Miguel Silva, Jo\~ao Vitorino, Daniela Pinto, Eva Maia, Ivone Amorim, Isabel Pra\c{c}a
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26824v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A Security Operations Center (SOC) plays a critical role in detecting, correlating, and responding to modern cyber threats. However, SOCs continue to face challenges related to alert overload, fragmented detection capabilities, and limited collaboration between analysts and automated systems. These issues often result in delayed incident response, analyst fatigue, and an increased risk of overlooking sophisticated, multi-stage attacks that unfold gradually across different layers of the network. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a unified framework for network traffic classification and alert correlation through the use of signature rules, machine learning, and sequential pattern mining algorithms. The solution was evaluated in a controlled testbed environment emulating realistic, multi-stage attack scenarios, including malware exploitation, lateral movement, reconnaissance, and data exfiltration. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in detecting and correlating complex attack behaviors, while providing analysts with actionable insights in line with a human-in-the-loop approach to SOC operations.

title: Compiling Existential-Positive Queries to Bounded-Variable Fragments
authors: Christoph Berkholz, Hubie Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26869v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A crucial property of bounded-variable fragments of first-order logic is that they can be evaluated in polynomial time. It is therefore a useful preprocessing step to rewrite, if possible, a first-order query to a logically equivalent one with a minimum number of variables. However, it may occur that reducing the number of variables causes an increase in formula size. We investigate this trade-off for the existential-positive fragment of first-order queries, where variable minimisation is decidable in general. In particular, we study the blow-up in the formula size when compiling existential-positive queries to the bounded variable fragment of positive first-order logic. While the increase of the formula size is always at most exponential, we identify situations (based on the signature and the number of variables) where only a polynomial blow-up is needed. In all other cases, we show that an exponential lower bound on the formula size of the compiled formula that matches the general upper bound. This exponential lower bound is unconditional, and is the first unconditional lower bound for formula size with respect to the studied compilation; it is proved via establishing a novel interface with circuit complexity which may be of future interest.

title: Extracting Next Generation Access Control Policies from Natural Language Using LLMs: An Intermediate-Representation Approach with Back-Translation Verification
authors: Ayesha Habib, Huixiang Zhang, Waiz Haider
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organizations write access-control rules in natural language, but NIST's Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) needs them as a formal policy graph. Large language models (LLMs) can automate this translation, but their output can break the format, add rules the text does not state, or drop conditions. We present NGAC-IR, which follows model-driven engineering (MDE). First, the LLM fills in an intermediate representation (IR), a JSON template that records who may, must or must not do what, on which resource and under which condition; a grammar keeps the output within this template. Second, a compiler that uses no LLM converts the IR into an NGAC policy graph and links each rule to its source sentence. Third, a back-translation check writes each rule in English and asks an LLM whether the source sentence states it. On four public datasets, all outputs could be compiled, compared with 95.5% without the grammar, and 95.7% were faithful to their sentence. NGAC-IR outperforms two published methods on all four datasets: the LLM-based Code4Policy in exact match and faithfulness, and the rule-based extractor of Abdelgawad et al. in rule type. The back-translation check sent 10.5% of sentences to human review and found 26 of the 31 errors. To test enforcement, we deployed the compiled policies in NIST's Policy Machine: they gave the expected decision for all 390 access requests, and the tested obligations were carried out. On one local server with open-weight models, all 714 sentences take about 20 minutes and 0.35 kWh, at zero API cost.

title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending
authors: Tarun Chitra, Manvir Schneider, Nagu Thogiti
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $\Theta(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.

title: Verification of Statistical Properties: Redefining the Possible
authors: Cl\'ement Canonne, Sam Polgar, Aditya Vikram Singh, Aravind Thyagarajan, Qiping Yang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We revisit the setting of Interactive Proof Systems for Distribution Testing, introduced by Chiesa and Gur (2018), showing that a simple twist on the task requirements may lead to dramatic improvements, allowing verifiers with constant sample complexity. We define and investigate the multi-prover and zero-knowledge versions of these interactive proof systems, using as flagship example the task of farness verification - the "dual" version of closeness testing. We hope our results will inspire others to investigate and analyze the power and limitations of multiple provers for distribution verification.

title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
authors: Zibin Lin, Taotao Wang, Shengli Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26983v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.

title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models via Perceptual Image Editing
authors: Haoyang Xu, Christian Iha, Colbren Fujimoto, Yingfei Dong, Rui Ning, Liuwan Zhu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.26987v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.

title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning in LLM Agents
authors: Shih-Chieh Dai, Xinyu Sun, Haichuan Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhong, Guanhong Tao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks hijack an LLM agent's workflow through malicious instructions embedded in retrieved external content. The growing adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) exposes another attack surface: tool descriptions supplied by third-party MCP servers. Attackers can manipulate this metadata to induce malicious argument generation during tool calls. The challenge is to ensure that the modified descriptions still appear benign to both LLMs and users. Existing IPI attacks, however, struggle to achieve both high attack success and low detectability in this setting. To address this challenge, we propose GRAFT, an LLM-based optimization method for crafting adversarial tool descriptions. Specifically, GRAFT uses a masking mechanism to identify argument-relevant token positions for targeted injection. It then iteratively refines candidate descriptions using dynamic mutation strategies proposed by an LLM, guided by the agent's tool choices and generated arguments. We evaluate GRAFT on three public datasets against several attack baselines. The results show that GRAFT achieves higher attack success while maintaining low detection rates across five filter-based defenses. It also bypasses several existing IPI defenses. Even under an adaptive defense trained on GRAFT-generated injections, GRAFT remains more effective than the baselines.

title: Railroads as Cyber-Physical Systems: Cybersecurity Implications of Increasing Automation -- Threats, Consequences, and Operational Resilience
authors: Syed Owais Athar, Mohsin Kamal, Aemal Khattak, Muhammad Naveed Aman
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27088v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objectives: Rail automation improves train protection, traffic management, inspection, and operational efficiency but increases dependence on software, communications, remote access, and external providers. This paper examines its impact on railroad cyber-physical system security and operational resilience.
  Methods: A narrative review synthesizes railroad automation literature, OT security guidance, FRA and TSA materials, and documented rail cyber incidents. Automation functions are mapped to exposed assets, attack vectors, and operational consequences, focusing on signalling, communications, onboard systems, remote access, and human oversight.
  Findings: Automation shifts rail risks from isolated mechanical failures toward interconnected cyber-physical dependencies. Key vulnerabilities involve train detection, positioning, signalling, grade crossings, remote diagnostics, vendor access, and AI-enabled monitoring. Cyber incidents can cause operational disruption, supply-chain impacts, and national-security risks, even when fail-safe mechanisms prevent catastrophic outcomes.
  Novelty: The paper introduces a rail-specific taxonomy connecting automation functions, cyberattack pathways, operational consequences, and resilience requirements, framing cybersecurity as an operational rather than purely IT concern.
  Practical Applications: The framework supports security-by-design procurement, IT/OT segmentation, secure remote access and software updates, degraded-mode planning, trusted recovery, and human oversight. Operators and regulators can use it to assess automation deployments and mitigate cyber risks.

title: "More Than You Expect!": Leakage-Abuse Attacks on Encrypted Vector Search
authors: Yang Zhang, Ruiqi He, Xiaoqian Sun, Siyi Lv, Zheli Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vector databases support semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embeddings, queries, and record labels may contain sensitive information. Although encrypted vector search protects these contents, some schemes expose records retrieved together across queries. We identify semantic neighborhood leakage, whereby co-retrieval relationships derived from access patterns reveal semantic categories of encrypted records and queries. We present SAGE (Semantic Access-pattern Graph Exploitation), a passive, persistent leakage-abuse attack that infers record labels and query categories from access patterns. SAGE builds a weighted co-retrieval graph and offers two variants requiring different auxiliary knowledge. SAGE-Dist matches anonymous spectral groups to semantic categories using estimated class proportions and refines labels via optimal transport, without known record labels. SAGE-Known combines graph-based label propagation with spectral-group anchor voting using a small set of known labels. We evaluate SAGE on four text and image datasets. With 1% known record labels, SAGE-Known achieves up to 84.3% mean record-label accuracy and outperforms the strongest corresponding baselines on all four datasets. With only estimated class proportions, SAGE-Dist achieves 66.9% record-label accuracy and 68.1% query-category accuracy on AG News, exceeding the strongest corresponding baselines by 21.8 and 41.9 percentage points, respectively, though performance varies across datasets. Experiments with a real-world DCPE implementation (Fuchsbauer et al., SCN'22) show that semantic leakage persists under encrypted approximate retrieval. These findings expose privacy risks even when vector contents remain protected.

title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
authors: Linru Zhang, Jun Jie Sim, Xiangning Wang, Jiahao Zhong, Kaiyu Zhou, Huanyi Ye, Yongsen Zheng, Lushan Song, Xiaojian Liang, Yingting Liu, Yujing Sun, Huaxiong Wang, Pu Duan, Kwok-Yan Lam
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27175v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these issues, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations. Additionally, we exploit functional bootstrapping to fold the evaluation of element-wise activation functions directly into the bootstrapping step, thereby reducing overall computational complexity. As a result, our framework achieves a $30\times$ reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across all matrix operations, as well as a $2.5\times$ reduction in FHE bootstrapping invocations over the entire computation flow, compared to the latest state-of-the-art work. It is worth noting that our system completes fine-tuning of a 2-layer BERT-style model with a batch size of 16 in 650 seconds, achieving a $8\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art work.

title: Enhancing Metaverse Security using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework
authors: Esha Kuppanda, Shalaka Mahadik, Pranav M. Pawar, Mithun Mukherjee, Raja Muthalagu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27199v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.

title: User-Irrepressible Sequences for Multiple-Packet Reception
authors: Yen-Ling Shih, Yuan-Hsun Lo, Yijin Zhang, Ying Miao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper studies deterministic transmission schemes based on protocol sequences for slot-synchronous multiple-packet reception (MPR) channels without feedback or synchronization of sequence phases. Each user schedules its transmissions according to a preassigned periodic binary sequence. A sequence set has the user-irrepressible property with MPR capability $\gamma$ ($\gamma$-UI) if every user is guaranteed at least one successful transmission per period, regardless of the relative cyclic shifts. We propose a unified explicit construction based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) for arbitrary MPR capability $\gamma\geq 2$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified CRT-based construction framework for $\gamma$-UI sequences over this full range, without requiring conflict-avoiding codes with prescribed parameters. We establish the $\gamma$-UI property through bounds on pairwise Hamming cross-correlations and show that suitably selected subsets support one additional active user without increasing the sequence length. We also derive exact average individual delay expressions over all possible cyclic shifts and extend the delay analysis to $\gamma$-UI sequence sets obtained from conflict-avoiding codes.

title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation
authors: Zixuan Wang, Zheng Tianyu, Yuan Lu, Bin Xiao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27250v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) support anonymous exercise of authority delegated through intermediaries, as in DeFi credit delegation. Existing DACs require holders to possess and process chain-shaped lineage material for presentation. We call this limitation \emph{prover awareness}: presentation cost grows with delegation depth, while holder-visible topology can enable lineage-based vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship.
  We formalize the privacy dimension as \emph{Enhanced Delegation Anonymity} (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness. We give simulation and indistinguishability formulations over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Our framework, \emph{Proof-Carrying Credentials} (PCC), addresses both limitations by replacing the explicit chain with a recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC). PCC makes presentation independent of delegation depth and hides topology beyond permitted leakage, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation.
  Unlike pairing-based constant-size DACs, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM using transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures. On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 instantiation keeps a constant 7.344\,KB verifier-facing proof with 35--36\,ms verification across all tested depths. The 128-bit Plonky2 instantiation keeps a constant 157.9\,KB proof with 3.8\,ms verification across depths $L\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$, at 1.03\,s per delegation step. These results demonstrate practical depth-independent presentation and holder-side topology hiding.

title: Proactive Defense Benchmark against Deepfake Generation
authors: Joonhyuk Baek, Wonjune Seo, Jae-yun Kim, Saerom Park, Hoki Kim
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27253v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite the proliferation of proactive defenses against deepfakes, the lack of a unified evaluation protocol precludes fair comparison and masks critical vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically assesses disruption, robustness, and transferability encompassing pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Our extensive analysis reveals that fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes, often leading to conflicting interpretations when relied upon individually. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental trade-off where peak white-box performance signals overfitting, and we introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct generator-induced identity bias. By exposing these blind spots, we establish a rigorous standard to guide the development of genuinely generalizable protections. Project page is available at: https://proactivedefensebenchmark.github.io/

title: Suspected Until Inspected: Neuro-Symbolic Detection of Broken Access Control in Server-Side Web Applications
authors: Chengyao Yang, Zifeng Kang, Dongqi Han, Shihong Zou
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Broken access control (BAC) has topped the OWASP Top 10 since 2021. Unfortunately, a decade of detectors still leaves a gap on every front. Static analyzers are tied to one language or framework, dynamic testers cover only the endpoints they manage to exercise, and LLM-based auditors leave the final verdict to an error-prone model. In this paper, we design and implement FLINT, a neuro-symbolic framework that detects BAC in server-side web applications without language- or framework-specific rules. Our key insight is to separate the proposal from the verdict -- an LLM may flag any data access as needing a guard, but only a symbolically verified check can clear it. The neural component enumerates every endpoint and distills each, via demand-driven code slicing, into an authorization certificate whose claims are all grounded in cited code. The symbolic component verifies each claimed check through origin tracing and a lattice-based interprocedural dataflow analysis, so that no access is cleared on the model's word. When applied to popular real-world open-source applications, including Gitea, Grafana, and Strapi, FLINT detected 112 zero-day, exploitable BAC vulnerabilities, 30 of them in projects with over 20,000 GitHub stars. We have responsibly disclosed all of them to the developers. Mattermost, for example, has already confirmed our report and is assigning a CVE identifier.

title: A Geometric Approach to the Classification of Locally-APN Niho-Type Power Functions
authors: Chenxu Wang, Jun Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27312v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Let $q=2^m$ with $m\geq 2$. We develop a geometric approach to the classification of locally-APN Niho-type power functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$. Our approach begins with a characterization of $\mathbb{F}_q$-homogeneous functions: the conditions $D_F(a,F(a))=q$ and $D_F(a,b)\leq 2$ for every $a\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$ and $b\neq F(a)$ hold if and only if the projective graph of $F$ is a $(q+1)$-arc in $\mathrm{PG}(3,q)$. For Niho-type power functions, this differential condition is equivalent to the locally-APN property. Applying the classification of $(q+1)$-arcs and the description of their stabilizers, we prove, for $m\geq 3$, that $F_s(x)=x^{s(q-1)+1}$ is locally-APN if and only if $s\equiv(2^k+1)^{-1}\pmod{q+1}$ for some $1\leq k\leq 2m-1$ satisfying $\gcd(k,m)=\gcd(2^k+1,q+1)=1$. Together with the known case $m=2$ and the sufficient condition of Xie et al., this gives the complete classification and confirms the conjecture of Cui, Luo, and Xiang.

title: Dual-Agent DRL based Cooperative Beamforming and Trajectory Optimization for UAV-ISAC Networks
authors: Kaijian Yang, Feng Wang, Guojun Han, Xin Wang, Vincent K. N. Lau
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27346v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper considers a low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) network, where multiple ground base stations (BSs) provide integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) services for multiple communication UAVs (C-UAVs) and sensing UAVs (S-UAVs). With the objective of maximizing the average sum rate of C-UAVs over the entire flight episode, we jointly optimize the multi-BS multi-UAV ISAC beamforming and trajectory design, subject to the BS transmit power budget and the sensing signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) constraints of S-UAVs, as well as the flight mission and collision avoidance constraints of C-UAVs and S-UAVs. Based on the multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) technique, we develop a dual-agent scheme, termed DeepDA-OPT, to solve the resulting constrained Markov decision process (MDP). In the proposed DeepDA-OPT scheme, two agents, i.e., Agent-B and Agent-T, are specifically deployed for learning the multi-BS ISAC transmit beamformers and the C-UAV/S-UAV trajectories, respectively, where the optimal BS receive beamformers for the sensing echo signals of S-UAVs are obtained in closed form by leveraging the generalized Rayleigh quotient theorem. To mitigate the overestimation of value functions, both Agent-B and Agent-T are trained based on the twin-delayed deep deterministic (TD3) policy-gradient algorithm. In addition, a constraint-aware noise exploration policy is employed, and the reward function is designed to incorporate a sensing penalty and a flight urgency penalty, thereby guiding the training of Agent-B and Agent-T. Numerical results show that, compared with the baseline schemes, the proposed DeepDA-OPT scheme achieves a higher average sum rate of C-UAVs, while the sensing SINR constraints are empirically well satisfied and no collision violation is observed under the evaluated settings.

title: Balanced Boolean Functions from Sparse Niho-Type Permutation Polynomials: Few-Valued Walsh Spectra and Applications
authors: Chenxu Wang, Jun Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27371v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study balanced Boolean functions parameterized by two-to-one mappings of the forms $P(x+x^2)$ and $P(x+x^{-1})$, where $P$ is a sparse permutation polynomial with generalized Niho-type exponents. First, for $q=2^m$ with $m$ even, we determine the complete four-valued Walsh distribution of the balanced Boolean function parameterized by $Q(x+x^2)$, where $Q(x)=x(1+x^{q-1}+x^{2(q-1)})$. We then generalize a permutation polynomial studied by Gupta and Sharma to the parameterized family $P_\lambda(x)=x^{3q-1}+\lambda x^{2q}+\lambda x^2$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$. We prove that $P_\lambda$ is a permutation polynomial if and only if either $\lambda=0$, or $\lambda\ne0$ and $X^3+X+\lambda^{-1}$ has no root in $\mathbb{F}_q$. Moreover, the number of admissible parameters is $(q+2)/3$ when $m$ is even and $(q+4)/3$ when $m$ is odd. Thus, admissible parameters exist for every $m\geq2$, and approximately one-third of the elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$ yield permutation polynomials. For every admissible parameter $\lambda$, we determine the complete Walsh distribution of the balanced Boolean function $f_\lambda$ parameterized by $P_\lambda(x+x^2)$ and prove that this distribution is independent of $\lambda$. For $m\geq3$, these functions have the five-valued Walsh spectrum ${q,0,-q,-2q,-3q}$, while for $m=2$ the spectrum degenerates to four values. As applications, their supports yield projective minimal binary five-weight codes, sets with five hyperplane intersection numbers, and regular cubelike Cayley graphs with six distinct eigenvalues. Finally, for mappings of the form $P(x+x^{-1})$, we construct an infinite family of balanced Boolean functions with simple explicit trace representations.

title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
authors: Ali Yousefi, Nikos Komninos, Hafizul Asad
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
authors: Ahaan Dabholkar, Harshvardhan Patel, Michalis Polychronakis, Saurabh Bagchi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
authors: Feng Huang, Qiang Huang, Yue Gao, Mei Zhang, Bin Liu, Lihua Ju, Xinhao Wei, Yongfeng Huang, Yu Qing, Yunqi Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27426v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

title: The Complexity of Fair and Stable Data Exchange
authors: Hannaneh Akrami, Bhaskar Ray Chaudhury
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27438v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data exchange is a fundamental challenge for Web applications such as recommender systems, personalized search, and fraud detection, where combining data across participants can improve predictions. Sustaining such collaboration requires fair returns for contributions and protection against groups leaving for a more beneficial exchange. These requirements are captured by reciprocity, which equates each participant's received utility with its credited contribution to others, and core stability, which rules out any coalition exchanging its own data to make every member strictly better off. Akrami et al. prove that such exchanges exist under broad assumptions, but leave efficient computation open. Two fundamental cases are submodular utilities, capturing diminishing returns from overlapping datasets, and supermodular utilities, capturing complementarities. We settle the approximate computation of reciprocal and core-stable exchanges in both cases, establishing a computational separation under Shapley sharing. For cross-monotone shares, which include Shapley shares under monotone submodular utilities, we give a circulation algorithm that computes an exactly core-stable, $\epsilon$-reciprocal exchange in time poly$(n,1/\epsilon,L)$ given efficient access to approximate shares, where $n$ is the number of participants and $L$ bounds how fast each donor's credit changes with its own contribution. This yields an FPTAS when $L$ is polynomially bounded. In contrast, finding an $\epsilon$-reciprocal, $\epsilon$-core-stable exchange is PPAD-hard for monotone lattice-supermodular utilities, even at inverse-polynomial accuracy, with constant $L$ and exact polynomial-time evaluation of Shapley shares. Thus overlapping information permits efficient fair and stable exchange, while complementarities create a computational barrier even when contribution credits are easy to evaluate.

title: Poisoning Attacks and Collaborative Defense Framework for LightRAG-Based Construction Regulation Knowledge
authors: Yingyan He
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27460v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used in construction, yet the security of building-regulation knowledge bases has received little study. This thesis reports a pre-registered experiment on one fully instrumented LightRAG system built on the UK Approved Documents. Using a 150-item benchmark labeled with safety consequences and tampering directions, it evaluates four attacks (text layer, graph layer, fabricated amendment narrative and a defense-aware adaptive attacker) together with a three-layer retrieval-graph-generation defense in a full factorial design. Text-level poisoning succeeded, with success rising with the budget; graph-level poisoning was less effective, contrary to the registered hypothesis. The full defense met the registered criterion and six of the seven configurations met its threshold, but those containing the generation layer did so by refusing 69-80 percent of poisoned queries, costing up to 74 points of clean accuracy, whereas provenance-based retrieval filtering cost no measurable clean accuracy in the configuration used. A second experimental batch showed that excluding a legitimate unregistered amendment caused no measurable loss of accuracy either, as its wording reached the generator through the graph's entity and relationship descriptions, the route the poison took, which no layer inspects. Interactions were strong, so no layer's contribution can be isolated. A reported zero attack success rate is not evidence of detection unless the refusal rate is reported with it: zero arises either because provenance filtering removes every document outside the manifest without judging its content, or because the system refuses. Layered defenses must therefore be evaluated factorially, and regulatory RAG assistants require corpus admission control and version-aware verification before they can support safety-critical decisions.

title: 3D-NAND-CIM: A Hybrid-Bonded 3D-NAND-Flash-based Analog In-Memory-Compute macro offering 4.8M weights/mm$^2$
authors: Pritish Narayanan, Athanasios Vasilopoulos, Geoffrey W. Burr, Manuel Le Gallo, Bill Filipiak, Hernan Castro, Jeremy Binfet, Jeremy Hirst, Henry Utomo, Kunal Parekh, Bharat Bhushan, Rajasekhar Venigalla, Kyle Kirby, Urs Egger, Jose Luquin, Vara Prasad Jonnalagadda, Athanasios Siampakos, Theodore Antonakopoulos, Kohji Hosokawa, Masatoshi Ishii, Yasuteru Kohda, Seiji Munetoh, Abhairaj Singh, Alexander Friz, Julian B\"uchel, Iason Chalas, Charles Mackin, Akul Malhotra, Akira Goda, Duane Mills, Gregory Atwood, Mark Helm, Jeffrey Burns, Vijay Narayanan, Hsinyu Tsai, Abu Sebastian
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27479v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We describe an analog-in-memory-compute macro hybrid-bonding a 14nm logic die onto a 3D NAND Flash memory wafer, achieving weight density of 4.8M weights/mm$^2$. Weights are programmed to 1-of-16 conductances. MACs with current-controlled oscillator ADCs show weight-equivalent precision between 3 and 4 bits for 8-bit inputs on multiple NAND tiers at energy efficiencies up to 4.2 TOPS/W. A charge-retention circuit improves accuracy, with $\sim$0.4% (3.23%) accuracy drop on a WideResNet for CIFAR-10 (100).

title: Mjolnir: Finding and Reproducing Vulnerabilities in Root-of-Trust Firmware and RTL with Project-Grounded Agents
authors: Collin MacDonald, Carl Lundin, Stephen Herwig, Miguel Osorio, Timothy Trippel
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27567v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A root of trust (RoT) anchors secure boot and attestation for the system above it, so a bug in RoT firmware or hardware undermines every layer that trusts it. LLM agents now find real vulnerabilities in general-purpose software, but RoT code presents two challenges. First, many security-relevant bugs depend on project-specific trust boundaries and fault-injection countermeasures rather than generic vulnerability patterns, and may cause no crash. Second, without RoT hardware, agents must exercise RoT inputs through the project's own hardware model, mocks, or RTL testbenches.
  We present Mjolnir, an agentic pipeline that supplies each project's threat model and design conventions to discovery and skeptical review agents, and reproduces surviving findings as proof-of-concept tests in the project's own toolchain. We evaluate Mjolnir on six firmware and RTL targets in Caliptra, OpenTitan, and OpenPRoT. On Caliptra's runtime firmware, it reaches 83.3%-100% precision across three models under blind expert labeling, including 100% on Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 66.7%-78.6% for four single-agent baselines on the same model. On 34 known security-relevant bugs in Caliptra's core firmware fixed after the models' training cutoffs, it finds 10 with Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 7 for the best baseline, and 17 with Gemini 4 Argon versus 12. Across our evaluation scans, maintainers have confirmed 64 of Mjolnir's findings as previously unknown security-relevant bugs: 37 across three models on Caliptra's runtime firmware and 27 across single scans of the other five targets.

title: Manipulation-resistant reputation for peer-to-peer scientific publishing: a combination-therapy approach
authors: Fr\'ed\'eric Prost
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27625v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In open peer-to-peer networks, where publishing is nearly free and identities are cheap, reputation systems decide what deserves attention, and their metrics become targets for manipulation. We study how to choose and combine reputation signals so that manipulation does not pay while genuine contribution does. Inspired by combination therapies in medicine, we describe each gaming action by its effects on all signals. For aggregation by the minimum of the signals, we prove that, in a global linear model, either some mix of gaming actions raises every signal by more than it costs, or the net gain of gaming is bounded by the imbalance of the attacker's honest profile; locally, gaming brings no first-order gain exactly when an admissible weighting is supported on the attacker's weakest signals. We then specify, without implementing it, MagMell, a two-tier system for peer-to-peer scientific publication: a protocol that orders signed events by Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus, enforces budgets and settles staked assessments, and open reputation algorithms that any node can run. Simulations on synthetic data show that minimum aggregation makes networks of fake identities, collusion rings and floods of generated papers lose rank beyond small intensities, at the price of a lower correlation between rank and quality for honest accounts. They also show that criticism is rarely settled, because the evidence needed is seldom available. The replicated log should grow by about 26 kilobytes per identity and year (analytic estimate), and a full recomputation of reputations takes 1.0 to 1.6 seconds for 100,000 identities (measured).

title: Too Fast to Doubt? Skipping Reasoning Leaves Jev-like Models Vulnerable
authors: Yue Li, Hao Wu, Zenan Fu, Xiao Li, Fengyuan Xu, Sheng Zhong
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27679v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fast decision models offer low-latency actions and explicit confidence estimates. We audit four state-of-the-art decision models on 1,440 paired synthetic browser tasks, injecting false conclusions or evidence interpretations through external comments. Across models, clean accuracy averages 91.0%, yet two-shot attack success reaches 81.2%. Mean expected calibration error rises from 2.6% on clean inputs to 36.7% under conclusion poisoning and 36.1% under evidence poisoning. Clean accuracy and calibration therefore do not ensure reliable decisions under injection. We further compare GPT-6 Luna and Luna Decisions, which share the same base model, on 48 matched tasks. With a chain of thought averaging fewer than 30 reasoning tokens per response, low-effort GPT-6 Luna answers 95.83% of poisoned inputs correctly, versus 38.54% for native Luna Decisions, while mean selected-generation latency increases from 0.29 to 1.94 seconds. These results expose a sharp latency-robustness trade-off: skipping reasoning for sub-second speed leaves fast decision models substantially more vulnerable to deceptive web content.

title: To Own or Not to Own? Endogenous Ownership in Peer-to-Peer Sharing of Private Autonomous Vehicles
authors: Xinling Li, Gioele Zardini
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27691v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous driving allows private owners to release their vehicles to an on-demand platform and earn income when they do not need them. This possibility changes vehicle acquisition incentives, as rental income can encourage purchases, while access to shared vehicles can reduce the need for personal ownership. Understanding these competing effects is essential to assessing the ownership implications of private AVs sharing. While existing models of private AV sharing often take ownership as given, in this paper, we develop a stationary equilibrium model in which vehicle ownership and listing decisions determine service availability and operational frictions, which in turn shape individuals' incentives to own and share. Based on the model, we first characterize individual choices by comparing payoffs of being an owner and a non-owner. We then analyze the resulting potential population partitions, establish conditions for the existence of an active sharing market, and categorize them by owner types. The equilibrium is presented by a system of equations and solved through a tailored algorithm. An illustrative numerical study on calibrated U.S. travel and vehicle cost data shows that sharing can either increase or decrease ownership, depending on the balance between purchases encouraged by rental income and ownership displaced by shared vehicles. The balance is shaped by market parameters, including market density, AV cost, and platform operating conditions. Platform pricing and municipal regulation can also influence ownership through their effects on acquisition incentives and the shared service that makes nonownership attractive. These findings highlight the range of possible ownership outcomes in private AV sharing markets, and the model provides a framework for evaluating how market conditions, platform decisions, and regulation shape these outcomes.

title: Coding Length and Optimal Power Allocation in Correlated Block Fading
authors: Haoran Xu, Huazhong Zhao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27694v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A codeword spans a fixed number of correlated Gaussian fading blocks. The receiver knows the gains and the transmitter knows only their law. At fixed average signal-to-noise ratio, we require the decoding error probability to decay exponentially with the number of receive antennas. When does outage predict the achievable rate? If block length grows faster than the number of antennas, outage gives the limiting optimal rate. If both grow to infinity at a fixed positive ratio of block length to array size, outage strictly overestimates the limiting rate. We determine the critical ratio above which positive rates are possible. For sufficiently large finite ratios, we find the exact limiting rate over all codes satisfying a total energy constraint on each codeword. The leading rate loss is inversely proportional to the ratio. Its coefficient depends on Gaussian channel dispersion at the most likely fade causing outage and on how quickly the outage rate decreases as the required error exponent increases. In the long-block limit, equal power loses rate on every window of three or more blocks under stationary first-order autoregressive fading with positive lag-one correlation. In a different three-block channel with identical marginal gains, tightening the reliability requirement first makes it optimal to leave the middle block unused and later to use it again.

title: Do Alice and Bob Dream of the Oracle? Wishful Cryptanalysis
authors: Guoxiao Liu, Keting Jia, Hongbo Yu, Zongyue Wang, Tianshuo Cong, Junfeng Fan, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27729v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For two millennia, offense and defense have forged cryptographic security boundaries. Tools automated calculation and search, while humans drove discovery. Foundation models now mark a shift from automated computation to intelligent scientific discovery. Because cryptanalysis rests on exact mathematical definitions and immediately executable truth, it offers a proving ground for autonomous intelligence to move past security reliant on scarce human attention and explore structures beyond human working memory. Unguided models stall between two opposite traps: authority hallucination, where they surrender whenever prior literature declares a route blocked, and reasoning hallucination, where they produce subtle, unverifiable flaws. Closed platforms and generic agent loops further impede sustained open inquiry. We introduce wishful cryptanalysis, a harness-agnostic methodology that pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification against error. Agents first compress reduced-scale theory within provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically. They then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory. Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models with minimal human intervention beyond targets and compute, this paradigm yielded novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES. These include breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released alongside an early-preview open-source workbench (agent-framework). Extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era, we envision an Open Oracle, an open and auditable public infrastructure that frees cryptographers to legislate security goals, challenge assumptions, distill theory, and co-design resilient standards.

title: Post-Quantum Migration in Brownfield 5G Core Networks: Verified Hybrid Key Establishment, Performance, and Rollback
authors: Shubham Verma
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27735v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Migrating brownfield 5G Core networks to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is difficult because deployed network functions, base images, and TLS libraries evolve under different upgrade constraints. This paper evaluates a deployment-controlled migration strategy that enables hybrid post-quantum/traditional key establishment through externally deployed Boundary Cryptographic Execution Entities (BCEEs), without modifying participating network function source code. The approach is evaluated using the Open5GS AMF-NRF Service-Based Interface as a representative 5G Core scenario. Classical and hybrid configurations are compared under an unchanged mediation topology. Packet-level analysis confirms successful negotiation of X25519MLKEM768, and functional validation demonstrates that representative SBI procedures remain operational through the mediated path. In 120 NF-registration transactions, the median AMF-facing registration latency increased from 22.968 ms under the classical state to 26.351 ms under the hybrid state, reflecting a 3.383 ms (14.73 percent) increase, with a whole-block 95 percent confidence interval of [1.193, 7.872] ms. At the mediated TLS boundary, the hybrid configuration shows a 4.599 ms higher median segment-local TLS-establishment time than the classical configuration. These two reported differences reflect system-level runtime effects and do not isolate key-encapsulation cost. Packet evidence verifies rollback from hybrid-mediated operation to classical mediated operation and, separately, restoration of the native direct path. NF-facing compatibility legs remained plaintext and outside the hybrid post-quantum scope. The results demonstrate a packet-verifiable and manually reversible brownfield mechanism for introducing hybrid post-quantum key establishment on a controlled 5G SBI segment.

title: Hardness of algorithmic Kadison-Singer problem from approximate hypergraph colouring
authors: Danny Vagnozzi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27740v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In 2015, Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava published a solution of a strong form of a conjecture by Weaver implying a positive answer to the Kadison-Singer problem - an open question of interest to several fields of pure and applied mathematics. Specifically, they proved that for all $\alpha>0$ and finite lists of vectors whose Euclidean norm is at most $\sqrt\alpha$ and whose outer products sum to the identity matrix, there exists a signed sum of these outer products whose operator norm is at most $\sqrt{8\alpha}+2\alpha$. Since then, significant effort has been put into understanding the algorithmic side of the Kadison-Singer problem; that is, the task of actually finding a signing resulting in a matrix with operator norm at most $c\sqrt\alpha$ for some fixed constant $c$. The first hardness results for this problem were proven independently by Spielman and Zhang [APPROX'22] and by Jourdan, Macgregor and Sun [ISAAC'23].
  In this short note, we prove that there exist values of $c$ arbitrarily close to $1$ such that it is NP-hard to distinguish indexed families of vectors for which there is a signed sum with operator norm equal to $0$ from those for which every signed sum has operator norm at least $c\sqrt\alpha$. This improves on the previous best bound by Spielman and Zhang. Our proof borrows significant ideas from the above mentioned hardness results, by adapting them to a reduction from the problem of approximating hypergraph colouring in the sense of promise constraint satisfaction problems.

title: $L^1$ stability of the entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$ without moment assumptions
authors: Norman El Fartass, Lampros Gavalakis, Ioannis Kontoyiannis
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27790v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We establish qualitative stability in $L^1$ and Ruzsa distance for Shannon's entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$, without any moment assumptions. The proof uses the optimal transport argument by Rioul (2017), majorization bounds of density rearrangements, and the stability of the sharp form of Young's inequality due to Christ (2019). Along the way we also extend recent one-dimensional results on de Bruijn's identity, the continuity of differential entropy, and the equality case of the entropy power inequality to random vectors of any dimension.

title: Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^{3/2}$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines
authors: A. R. Balasubramanian, Rupak Majumdar
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27814v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $\epsilon >0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{\frac{3}{2}-\epsilon})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{\frac{3k}{2}-\epsilon})$, where $N$ is the input size.
  Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.

title: BinXSight: Fast Binary Program Summarization via Hierarchical Modular Decomposition
authors: Zhijie Liu, Zhipeng Xue, Zhipeng Gao, Pengfei Jing, Zixiong Qin, Sen Nie, Shi Wu, Liang Feng Zhang, Yutian Tang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27816v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Binary code summarization (BCS) is crucial in fields such as cybersecurity. Particularly, program-level BCS can quickly provide a comprehensive overview of an entire stripped binary without in-depth manual reverse engineering. However, a binary often contains numerous functions with complex interactions, making it challenging to extract its functionality efficiently. Moreover, existing methods focus solely on function-level without considering contextual information, limiting their applicability to program-level analysis. Towards comprehensive and fast program-level BCS, we propose BinXSight, an LLM-powered framework based on hierarchical modular decomposition. Specifically, we first propose binary graph, a new data structure composed of four graphs, to comprehensively represent a binary. Then, based on the binary graph, we hierarchically decompose functions into modules and select the most significant ones. Finally, BinXSight generates a program-level summary from these module summaries. We evaluate BinXSight on stripped binaries across various sizes, fields, platforms, and architectures. Results show that BinXSight outperforms baselines by 23.18% to 46.99%, and summarizes a binary with about 3K functions in 24.3 seconds on average. In addition, a user study with 27 experts shows that BinXSight's high-quality summaries help users quickly understand the whole binary. Our case analysis on recent real-world malware further demonstrates its practical utility.

title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
authors: Nathan Nour Houlamy, Mattia Favretto, Earlence Fernandes, Mauro Conti
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27860v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed.
  Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

title: Metadata-Private Voice Communication over Tor using Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation
authors: Noah Zeinali Yazdi, Samuel Zeinali Yazdi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27909v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Encrypted voice communication systems commonly protect call content but expose significant metadata, including the network identities of both parties, call timing, and traffic patterns. Simultaneously, advances in quantum computing threaten the asymmetric primitives underlying conventional key exchange, creating a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk for long-lived sensitive communications. Existing systems address at most one of these concerns: secure VoIP applications such as Signal and Wire rely on centralized infrastructure and classical cryptography, while anonymous communication tools built on the Tor network support only text messaging and lack post-quantum key encapsulation. This paper presents SAPEC (Secure Anonymous Peer Exchange Communicator), a peer-to-peer voice communication system that simultaneously addresses anonymity, decentralization, and quantum resistance. SAPEC routes all traffic exclusively through Tor hidden services, concealing the IP addresses of both parties, and augments the standard TLS handshake with a custom protocol layer that performs ML-KEM-1024 key establishment, a settle on AES-256 symmetrical keys and mutual Dilithium identity verification before any audio is transmitted. All audio is subsequently encrypted under AES-256. A removable Crypto Ignition Key prevents identity key material from being stored on the device. Empirical evaluation across 45 independently circuit-rebuilt test runs yielded a median one-way audio delay of 355 milliseconds and a median connection setup time of 7.61 seconds on same-region Tor circuits, demonstrating that interactive voice communication over onion routing is practically achievable.

title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models
authors: Xuyang Liu, Zhiwei Xu, Zirui Li, Jiabao Gao, Xiaolin Peng, Weixian Deng, Tian Qiu, Hai Wan, Xibin Zhao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27920v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural network weights are usually treated as opaque artifacts of gradient descent. Recent work on weight space programming, however, suggests that large language models can inspect and rewrite another network's parameters directly. In this paper, we ask whether a general language model can turn a natural language backdoor specification into persistent, selective weight edits on its own, without gradient training, layer hints, external corpora, or a prescribed editing formula. Using DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort inside a restricted workspace that blocks local CPU simulation, we test three open models (Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, SmolLM3-3B) across two review domains (IMDb and Yelp; 18 independent sessions). Evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, the modified checkpoints reach 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain and 97.6% transfer success on the unseen domain, while preserving clean accuracy, low control drift, and general capabilities within 1.7 points of the base models. Our traces show that the model converges on edits in the final layer in 17 of 18 runs and discovers both dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery at an average cost of \$1.74 per run.

title: Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata
authors: Guangyuan Ji, Wenjing Wang, Bingsheng Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To prevent motion sensors from acting as covert microphones, Android 12+ caps SensorManager gyroscope and accelerometer rates at 200 Hz by default, requires HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS for higher rates, and throttles sensors back to 200 Hz when the microphone toggle is off. We show that Android's Camera2 subsystem bypasses these defenses. During an active Camera2 session, Camera HAL stabilization pipelines record high-rate gyroscope measurements and export them via vendor CaptureResult metadata. Loudspeaker speech excites chassis vibrations that couple into this path. Across 50 smartphones (2020-2026) from 10 vendors, 37 expose gyroscope metadata via Camera2, and 26 exceed 200 Hz--including six flagship models at 800-1000 Hz, double SensorManager's 400-500 Hz ceiling. This channel requires neither RECORD_AUDIO nor HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS and defeats privacy switches: turning off the microphone toggle does not throttle metadata, and turning off the camera toggle blanks only video frames while 800-1000 Hz metadata keeps streaming.
  To build a zero-profiling attack that generalizes to unseen phones, we introduce Source-to-Leakage Learning (S2L). Prior attacks train on real sensor traces, entangling speech with a specific phone's mechanical resonances and sampling rate. S2L decouples speech content from hardware acoustics using a physics-constrained forward simulator. Trained exclusively on simulated leakage without target-phone traces, our universal recognizer CamEar achieves 52.1% mean word accuracy (up to 61.8%) and 74.3% character accuracy (up to 80.7%) across the six 800-1000 Hz phones. In contrast, ISpyU models fine-tuned on real target-phone data drop to 25.9% word accuracy on unseen phones; CamEar improves cross-device accuracy by 101.4% and outperforms ISpyU's same-device models on every tested phone.

title: Recognizing $k$-inducible Digraphs is NP-complete
authors: Felix Brandt, Fabian Frank
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27965v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A digraph is k-inducible if its arcs correspond to the pairwise majority relation of a preference profile with k voters. By McGarvey's theorem, every asymmetric digraph is k-inducible for some k, but for every fixed k there are digraphs that are not k-inducible. Whether a digraph is 1-inducible or 2-inducible can easily be decided in polynomial time. The complexity of deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible for every fixed $k\geq 3$ has been a long-standing open problem. We prove that deciding whether a tournament is 3-inducible is NP-complete and then leverage this result to show that deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible is NP-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. Our results imply that, unless P=NP, k-inducible digraphs cannot be characterized by finitely many forbidden induced subdigraphs.

title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail
authors: Eleni Batziou, John Fearnley, Alexandros Hollender, Rahul Savani
abstract:
arXiv:2611.27977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the time complexity of finding a Tarski fixed point. We provide a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line (UEOPL) problem to the problem of finding a Tarski fixed point. Using a range of known cryptographic lower bounds for UEOPL, our reduction implies a range of conditional lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm that finds a Tarski fixed point. The strongest of these give quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds for the problem. We also obtain a similar quasi-polynomial-time lower bound for Tarski based instead on a weak exponential-time type hypothesis for UEOPL. These running time lower bounds match the recently discovered quasi-polynomial query lower bounds for the problem.

title: Nanoscale single-electron box with a floating lead for quantum sensing: modelling and device characterization
authors: Nikolaos Petropoulos, Xutong Wu, Andrii Sokolov, Panagiotis Giounanlis, Imran Bashir, Mike Asker, Dirk Leipold, Andrew K. Mitchell, Robert B. Staszewski, Elena Blokhina
abstract:
arXiv:2404.15002v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We present an in-depth analysis of a single-electron box (SEB) biased through a floating node technique that is common in charge-coupled devices (CCDs). The device is analyzed and characterized in the context of single-electron charge-sensing techniques for integrated silicon quantum dots (QD). The unique aspect of our SEB design is the incorporation of a metallic floating node, strategically employed for sensing and precise injection of electrons into an electrostatically formed QD. To analyse the SEB, we propose an extended multi-orbital Anderson impurity model (MOAIM), adapted to our nanoscale SEB system, that is used to predict theoretically the behaviour of the SEB in the context of a charge-sensing application. The validation of the model and the sensing technique has been carried out on a QD fabricated in a fully depleted silicon on insulator (FDSOI) process on a 22-nm technological node. We demonstrate the MOAIM's efficacy in predicting the observed electronic behavior and elucidating the complex electron dynamics and correlations in the SEB. The results of our study reinforce the versatility and precision of the model in the realm of nanoelectronics and highlight the practical utility of the metallic floating node as a mechanism for charge injection and detection in integrated QDs. Finally, we identify the limitations of our model in capturing higher-order effects observed in our measurements and propose future outlooks to reconcile some of these discrepancies.
